The Gold tegu, Tupinambis teguixin, is a large-bodied neotropical lizard for which a suite of physiological and life-history measurements have been gathered under controlled thermal regimes. In respirometry trials conducted at a metabolic chamber temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the species displays a maximum basal metabolic rate of approximately 2.4681 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = approximately 2.4681 milliliters of oxygen per minute]. This relatively elevated oxygen consumption reflects the high energetic demands typical of active, wide-foraging teiid lizards. When eggs are incubated at a constant 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the time required for embryonic development culminates in hatching after 90 days [ab = 90 days], a duration that aligns with the protracted incubation periods reported for other large teiids. Neonates emerge from the shell at a wet body mass of roughly 10 grams [Wwb = roughly 10 grams], a value inferred from comparative data on the closely related Argentine black and white tegu, Salvator merianae, given the difficulty of obtaining sufficient wild-born mass records for Tupinambis teguixin at the moment of hatching.

As the Gold tegu progresses through its early life stages, growth proceeds rapidly under favorable thermal conditions. From the moment of emergence, the juvenile period is characterized by intensive feeding and somatic expansion, with individuals eventually approaching a maximum adult body mass of 4000 grams [Wwi = 4000 grams]. This ultimate wet weight represents a substantial size, placing Tupinambis teguixin among the larger members of its genus and reflecting a life history that prioritizes the attainment of a large body frame before the energetic demands of reproduction begin. Field records and captive observations indicate that individuals maintained at an ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] can achieve a maximum lifespan of approximately 16.1 years [am = approximately 16.1 years], a longevity that is notable for a reptile of this body size and that implies a relatively slow pace of senescence compared to smaller teiid species. The interplay between thermal environment and longevity remains an area of active investigation, as temperature is known to modulate metabolic rate and, consequently, the rate of physiological aging.

Reproductive maturation in the Gold tegu is tightly linked to thermal conditions, with females reared at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C] exhibiting onset of gonadal activity at approximately 27 months after hatching [tp = approximately 27 months after hatching], though individual variation is considerable, with some sources reporting a range of 18 to 36 months for this transition. This time to sexual maturity is a key life-history parameter that influences the generation time and population dynamics of the species. Under this same thermal regime, the maximum reproductive output of the Gold tegu can be characterized by examining both the number of offspring produced per event and the frequency of those events. Females typically deposit a clutch ranging from 20 to 50 eggs per nesting event [N_R_i = 20 to 50 eggs per nesting event], and under optimal conditions, they are capable of producing approximately 1 to 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 clutches per year], although such frequencies are likely only achievable in captive settings with abundant food resources.

The interplay between developmental rates and incubation temperature is critical for understanding the Gold tegu's life-history strategy. Eggs incubated at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] require approximately 90 days [ab = approximately 90 days] to hatch, a duration consistent with the thermal dependence of embryogenesis observed across the family Teiidae, where cooler temperatures prolong development but may enhance hatchling viability. Hatchlings emerge weighing approximately 10 grams [Wwb = approximately 10 grams] and begin exogenous feeding almost immediately, initiating a period of rapid mass gain that, under optimal conditions, allows them to reach the 4000-gr(4000 grams [Wwi = 4000 grams]) am adult mass within several years. The substantial body size achieved by adults not only influences their metabolic rate, with a recorded maximum of 2.4681 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = 2.4681 milliliters of oxygen per minute] at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], but also dictates their ecological role as mesopredators within their South American habitats, where they consume a diverse array of prey including invertebrates, small vertebrates, fruits, and carrion.
